title: Why You Must Train
author: Thinking West
summary: Thinking West argues that the modern nerd-versus-jock split between intellectual and physical life would have been unrecognizable to the philosophers who built Western civilization, using Socrates and Plato as evidence that classical thought treated the mind-body connection as a civic duty rather than a personal hobby. Drawing on Xenophon's Memorabilia, the piece recounts Socrates scolding a physically weak young man by explaining that every male Athenian citizen owed his community battle-readiness, since untrained men were more likely to die or be enslaved when war came, and connects that duty to Socrates's own documented service and battlefield courage as a hoplite. It extends the argument through Plato, a competitive wrestler at the Isthmian Games, who wrote in The Republic that the ideal state's guardians must be simultaneously philosophers and warriors, strong as well as wise. The piece then translates this ancient civic-duty framing into a modern register, arguing that even though organized warfare is rare for most people today, physical readiness remains a duty owed to family and community, since fitness enables one to escape danger, deter predation, and remain a provider rather than a burden. It closes on an explicitly moral register, framing bodily neglect as a failure to use one's body to its fullest rather than a purely personal choice.
points: Grounds the mind-body connection in a specific primary-text scene (Xenophon's Memorabilia) rather than a general claim, showing Socrates directly scolding a physically neglectful young man by tying weakness to the real risk of death or enslavement in war.

Cites Alcibiades's own testimony that Socrates saved his life at the Battle of Potidaea, using contemporary eyewitness evidence rather than legend to establish that Socrates practiced the physical duty he preached.

Uses Plato's own definition of the ideal state's 'guardians' in The Republic - simultaneously philosophers and warriors, passionate and strong - to show the mind-body duty was a structural requirement for leadership in classical political theory, not an incidental biographical detail about individual philosophers.

Translates an ancient, war-specific civic duty into a modern, non-military register: physical readiness as the capacity to escape danger, deter predation, and remain a provider rather than a dependent burden on one's family.

Frames bodily neglect as a duty failure rather than a private lifestyle choice, explicitly rejecting the modern discomfort with the word 'duty' as itself part of what has eroded the classical mind-body connection.
quotes: No man has the right to be an amateur in the matter of physical training. It is a shame for a man to grow old without seeing the beauty and strength of which his body is capable.

they are not a few who, owing to a bad habit of body, either perish outright in the perils of war, or are ignobly saved. Many are they who, being taken prisoners, must endure the pains of slavery for the rest of their days

He trained and fought as a hoplite, the Greek infantry, and is recorded to have fought in at least three battles. He was even praised for his physical courage by Alcibiades at the Battle of Potidaea in 432 BC.

Anyone who is going to be a truly good guardian of our community, then, will have a philosopher's love of knowledge, and will be passionate, quick on his feet, and strong. And our guardians are, in fact, both warriors and philosophers.
Though physical combat is far less likely for your average person today, this does not mean that physical readiness is not a duty anymore. There are still dangers lurking about.
It's also a duty to remain healthy for your family and community so that you can continue to be useful. You need to be an asset to them rather than a burden.

We don't like to hear the word duty in the modern world, and our society has done almost everything it can to absolve us from our duties, but ultimately I do think it is your duty to remain physically capable as long as you can.
